shared: Create a refined petroleum mudlogging teaching illustration for a university web lesson. Landscape 3:2 composition. Detailed, physically plausible equipment, clear material textures, restrained watercolor-gouache technical editorial style with fine linework, warm ivory background, slate blue machinery and muted green accents. It must explain the specified single operation at a glance, not a generic oilfield panorama. No humans, no text, no letters, no numbers, no labels, no arrows, no circles, no highlight boxes, no watermark. Fill the composition with the relevant operation rather than empty space. Avoid decorative dashboards, floating icons, underground geology, drill towers, and science fiction. All reading labels and transparent highlight overlays will be added by code outside the artwork.

cases.prompt: Subject: surface collection of rock cuttings for lithology examination. Three-quarter close view of a shale shaker and a clean adjacent sampling bench. At the left, a sloping industrial vibrating screen receives brown drilling returns, separates coarse angular grey and tan rock fragments; liquid drains into a steel trough below. At the center and right foreground, a steel sampling scoop, wire rinse sieve over a basin, and two shallow white sample trays with a small number of clearly visible, washed angular chips, a hand lens resting next to the trays. Everything on one continuous practical work surface, visibly separating dirty returns from clean rock samples. The two trays and rinse sieve should occupy the central 45 percent of the composition, clearly readable and unobstructed. Do not include computers or UV lights. The teaching point is that screening, washing and sample identity precede photographing and classifying each grain.

Subject: mud gas sampling at the surface, from returning drilling mud to gas analysis. A clear close three-quarter view of a small open returning-mud trough along the lower left. A believable vertical cylindrical mud gas trap/extractor, with a motorized agitator head above it, is partly immersed in the moving muddy liquid. A thin translucent sample hose emerges from the sealed top of the extractor and runs visibly to the right, through a small transparent moisture trap/filter jar, then into a compact unbranded gas-analysis instrument on a dry workbench at the right. Keep the entire sampling hose unbroken and traceable, gas instrumentation dry and separate from the open mud trough. The gas trap, thin hose and moisture trap occupy the central 65 percent of the image; the analyzer is a small reference at far right with no data or readable display. No rock trays, no ultraviolet lamp. The teaching point is extraction and transport of sampled gas to the instrument, not a gas plume in the air.

Subject: paired white-light and ultraviolet observation of the same cuttings specimen. A close three-quarter view of a clean mudlogging sample bench. On the left is a white-light inspection station with a small articulated white lamp illuminating a shallow rectangular tray of angular pale grey and tan rock chips. On the right is a dark hooded ultraviolet viewing cabinet with its front inspection opening visible, containing a matching tray of chips in the same spatial arrangement. Only a few small patches in that tray exhibit subdued pale yellow-green fluorescence under purple illumination; most rock remains dark. Include a small neutral calibration strip beside each tray, with no text. The right cabinet observation opening is centered at approximately 67 percent across and 55 percent down the composition, large and unobstructed. No drill rig, no gas equipment, no biological specimens, no glowing crystals. This is an illustrative optical setup; do not make claims about real oil content.

Subject: the source of surface drilling parameter records, a realistic driller monitoring station. Three-quarter close view of a sturdy slate-blue industrial console, seen at working height. The console has three clearly distinct large round analog gauges on an upper panel and small blank digital readout modules underneath, physically mounted instruments for force/weight, rotary speed and fluid circulation. There is no text, no numbering, no tick labels on gauges. Below the panel are practical wired signal connections passing into an adjacent modest data acquisition box at the center foreground. On the dry desk at right is a single unbranded monitor showing only three plain continuous thin line traces on an empty light grid, no axes or labels or claims; a keyboard and a simple paper log sheet with faint horizontal rules. The wired acquisition box and the monitor form the main focal area across the middle and right, with plenty of equipment detail visible. No generic office scene, no rig or rock cutaway. The teaching point is that measured operating parameters are recorded together before comparing drilling responses by depth; the actual data plots are supplied separately by the webpage.

Subject: organizing mudlogging source records into a traceable report. Overhead editorial still life of a practical petroleum logging desk, one continuous scene. At the left are three neatly separated source folders with visible sheets: one has a small pasted rock-chip photograph, one has several thin time-series lines, and one has ruled handwritten-note-like strokes without any legible words. At center is an open cream logbook with orderly ruled columns and a small metal clip. At the right is a laptop showing a clean light document layout with short grey paragraph lines and a narrow source-reference sidebar, all deliberately abstract and without letters or numbers. A single paper report page in the lower center has restrained empty field boxes. Warm neutral desk surface, careful spacing, matte paper texture, no piles or clutter, no floating icons. The source folders and the report page should remain readable as distinct physical artifacts. The teaching point is relating each report sentence back to source notes, depth/unit fields and evidence, not inventing new geological conclusions.
